title: Duplicate replacement ballot raises new questions
summary: A duplicate ballot arriving at one Maryland home is raising new questions about a batch of replacement mail-in ballots rushed out to more than 400,000 state voters last month, after an error was discovered in the original mailing.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters June 9, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters June 9, 2026

A duplicate ballot arriving at one Maryland home is raising new questions about a batch of replacement mail-in ballots sent to more than 400,000 voters.

The replacement mail-in ballots were rushed to voters last month after it was discovered that the state’s printer had mistakenly sent some Democratic and Republican voters the ballot for the wrong party. But in the rush, at least one voter received two replacement ballots.

New concerns about the replacement ballots arose last week. A family member of a Maryland Matters reporter received two new ballots in three days. Both ballots are marked as replacements.

State Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis said last week that the duplication could be the result of a damaged ballot that was reprinted and mailed. He could not say why the duplicate was sent or if it was a singular instance. He asked for time to research the issue as well as to see if other voters were affected.

DeMarinis was not available for an interview Monday. A spokesperson for the agency did not provide answers to written questions.

The five-member board of elections is scheduled to meet on Tuesday. That meeting was scheduled on May 28.

Trump administration moves swiftly on plans to restrict voting by mail in the states

Nikki Tyree, executive director of the League of Women Voters, said “somebody is making a poor decision over there [at the Board of Elections] about how to communicate with the voters.”

“That will always shake confidence,” Tyree said. “You can see it in so many places. Once voters feel like their votes aren’t really counted, or they are being disenfranchised in any capacity, they just stop voting.”

The new concerns come a moment of heightened partisan scrutiny and criticism of mail-in voting.

Three weeks ago, President Donald Trump blasted the state board in a post on his Truth Social account. In that post, Trump said he would ask the Department of Justice to open an investigation.

Elections advocates said they were already concerned about potential federal intervention in elections, including the potential for federal immigration officers near polls and seizure of ballots.

Legal challenges are also a possibility. Maryland and the Department of Justice are already locked in a legal battle over voter registration information, with a hearing scheduled Wednesday on that case in federal court in Baltimore.

More than 565,000 voters who signed up to vote by mail received ballots as part of a first-round of mailings. That number includes voters — many of whom are members of the military serving overseas — who elect to print their ballot, mark it and mail it back.

The initial snafu was caused by the printer, which made a mistake in packing the ballots that led to some voters getting a primary ballot for the opposite party. Election officials and the printer could not identify who was affected.

DeMarinis at the time said not all voters who requested mail-in ballots were affected. Still, it was impossible to identify who or how many people were affected in the first round. The fix was to mail out more than 400,000 replacement ballots.

Those ballots were printed under the supervision of an official from Maryland, DeMarinis said during the May 28 Board of Elections meeting.

Taylor Print & Visual Impressions sent out the new ballots and mailings alerting voters at no cost to the state.

Glen Taylor, a billionaire and former Minnesota Republican senator, is founder, and chairman of the company and majority owner of the business. He also is the owner of the Minnesota Star Tribune newspaper.

The printing company did not respond to a request for comment.

Some voters have expressed confusion because of the replacement ballots.

“I think that ultimately we need to keep turning our eyes back to the voter experience, and right now the voter experience is one of deep confusion,” Tyree said. “Just being told to vote the replacement ballot clearly isn’t going to work in this situation.”

She worries that some voters will ultimately decide not to cast their primary ballot. Elections officials need to be willing to provide clear answers to questions the public might have, she said.

“I think ultimately confidence can be saved here as long as SBE remains open and honest,” Tyree said.

She characterized official explanations offered so far as a “high level, elitist thing.” That leads to misinformation, she said.

“I think how you honestly combat misinformation, you just keep talking about the correct information, and SBE seems unwilling to do that right now, and I don’t understand why,” Tyree said.

Tyree renewed calls for an outside review of the issue.

“I think we need to, we need to have one done,” she said. “I’m still not clear on whether Taylor has really been held to account for what they did. From what I understand, SBE has done its own internal investigation to make sure that it wasn’t a staffing problem. But is Taylor being held … to the same standard? If the answer is no, that’s a disservice to the voters. We deserve to know if Taylor has messed something up along the way, or if something really nefarious happened.”

DeMarinis, at the May 28 board meeting, downplayed the need for an independent review. He told the five-member board then that the issue will be part of a “lessons learned” look back after the primary.

That review is unsatisfying to Tyree.

“[Expletive] ‘lessons learned,” said Tyree. “This is so far beyond their lessons learned. This is a situation where we need an independent investigation, whatever that means. The General Assembly needs to be looking into this.”

Tyree said she is willing to give state elections officials the benefit of the doubt. An outside review could add credibility.

“I truly believe that this whole situation was outside of SBE’s control,” she said. “I would like an independent investigation to have some evidence to back up my belief.”

In the end, she said: “No state agency should ever be in a situation where they are investigating themselves.”
